item.content:encoded:
A Pensacola man accused of sexually abusing a child over a 10-year period has been ordered held in jail without bond pending trial, according to Miramar News. A judge determined the defendant poses a danger to the community and is not eligible for release.

The case involves allegations spanning a substantial period, though specific details about the charges, the defendant's name, and the child's identity have not been disclosed in available reports. The decision to hold without bond is typically reserved for cases where judges find clear and convincing evidence that an accused person presents a significant risk to public safety or is likely to flee.

The defendant remains in custody as the case moves toward trial. Additional details about the charges and timeline of the alleged abuse are expected to emerge through the judicial process.

item.title: PLT launches first Holiday Cabaret & Boutique Dec. 4–6 at Clark Center
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Pensacola Little Theatre is combining shopping, Santa photos, and live entertainment into a single holiday event this December. The first-ever Holiday Cabaret & Boutique runs Friday, Dec. 4 through Sunday, Dec. 6 at the Clark Family Cultural Center (400 S. Jefferson St.) and features up to 16 local vendors selling handmade ornaments,…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola Little Theatre is combining shopping, Santa photos, and live entertainment into a single holiday event this December. The first-ever Holiday Cabaret & Boutique runs Friday, Dec. 4 through Sunday, Dec. 6 at the Clark Family Cultural Center (400 S. Jefferson St.) and features up to 16 local vendors selling handmade ornaments, Pensacola-themed jewelry, regional art, stationery, and holiday décor—all without requiring a ticket to browse.

The boutique opens two hours before each evening's cabaret performance and stays open through intermission, giving shoppers time to browse and grab hot chocolate before catching a family-friendly Christmas show on the Mainstage. Friday and Saturday events run from 5:30 PM (boutique opens) to 7:30 PM (show), while Sunday's schedule moves earlier, with the boutique opening at 12:30 PM and the show at 2:30 PM.

Sandy Cox, executive director of Pensacola Little Theatre, said the goal was creating a one-stop holiday destination where families could support local makers while enjoying live performances. "Every dollar goes back into the community's theatre," Cox said. All proceeds benefit PLT and the Clark Family Cultural Center.

For tickets and details, visit pensacolalittletheatre.com or call 850-432-2042. Pensacola Little Theatre, a nonprofit serving Northwest Florida since 1936, also offers musicals, comedies, dramas, and youth and adult acting classes throughout the year.

item.content:encoded: The National Weather Service in Mobile has issued a Marine Warning for waters stretching from Pensacola to Pascagoula, Mississippi, effective Wednesday evening. The warning covers waters between 20 and 60 nautical miles offshore and calls for wind speeds exceeding 34 knots, with a possible waterspout. No hail is currently expected. The warning cancels an earlier marine alert for the same region and continues warnings for other areas farther east. Mariners in the affected zone are advised to exercise caution and monitor conditions closely.

item.title: Sen. Moody Introduces Bill to Move Federal Student Loans to Treasury Department
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: U.S. Senator Ashley Moody introduced legislation Wednesday aimed at streamlining federal student aid administration by transferring the Department of Education's loan portfolio to the Department of the Treasury, according to a press release from her office. The "Less Bureaucracy, Better Student Aid Act" reflects what Moody characterizes as a…
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Senator Ashley Moody introduced legislation Wednesday aimed at streamlining federal student aid administration by transferring the Department of Education's loan portfolio to the Department of the Treasury, according to a press release from her office.

The "Less Bureaucracy, Better Student Aid Act" reflects what Moody characterizes as a commonsense approach to reducing government bureaucracy. "Washington has long had a spending and bureaucracy problem—and one area where we especially see this is in student loans," Moody said in a statement. "My new legislation would simply transfer student loan functions from the Department of Education to the Department of Treasury, which already handles our government's finances."

Senator Jim Banks signed on as an original cosponsor. The measure is part of a broader legislative effort to reform Department of Education operations and return more education authority to individual states. The bill has drawn support from conservative advocacy groups including Heritage Action, Concerned Women for America, and Parents Defending Education Action, all of which argue that Treasury is better positioned to manage the federal government's $120 billion-plus annual student aid distribution.

item.title: Escambia County Fire Rescue: Follow Safety Tips to Prevent Thanksgiving Cooking Fires
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: As Pensacola-area families prepare Thanksgiving meals today, Escambia County Fire Rescue is urging residents to practice fire safety in the kitchen. Thanksgiving is the peak day nationally for home cooking fires, with the National Fire Protection Association reporting an estimated 1,139 such fires on Thanksgiving Day alone in 2024—more than three…
item.content:encoded:
As Pensacola-area families prepare Thanksgiving meals today, Escambia County Fire Rescue is urging residents to practice fire safety in the kitchen. Thanksgiving is the peak day nationally for home cooking fires, with the National Fire Protection Association reporting an estimated 1,139 such fires on Thanksgiving Day alone in 2024—more than three times the daily average.

Unattended cooking is the leading cause of kitchen fires and fire deaths, according to fire officials. ECFR recommends never leaving food unattended while the stove is on. If a pan catches fire, residents should place a lid over it, turn off the heat, and let it cool rather than panic. For oven fires, keep the door closed and turn off the oven to contain the flames.

Other kitchen fire prevention tips include keeping pot handles turned toward the back of the stove to avoid accidental bumping, wearing fitted clothing while cooking, and clearing the cooking area of flammable materials like paper towels and packaging.

For those planning to deep-fry a turkey, ECFR stresses using the fryer outdoors on a level, noncombustible surface at least 10 feet from buildings, keeping children and pets away, and ensuring the turkey is fully thawed and dried before frying to prevent dangerous oil splattering. The propane tank should be at least 2 feet from the burner, and the fryer should never be moved while in use.

item.title: Escambia County EMS CORE Program Reaches 850-Patient Recovery Milestone
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Escambia County Emergency Medical Services announced Wednesday that its Coordinated Opioid Recovery Effort program has successfully assisted its 850th patient since launching locally in early 2023, marking a significant achievement in the county's response to the opioid crisis. The CORE program, state-funded and expanded to Escambia County in late…
item.content:encoded:
Escambia County Emergency Medical Services announced Wednesday that its Coordinated Opioid Recovery Effort program has successfully assisted its 850th patient since launching locally in early 2023, marking a significant achievement in the county's response to the opioid crisis.

The CORE program, state-funded and expanded to Escambia County in late 2022, accepted its first patient in February 2023. The initiative combines emergency medical response with community resources including addiction counseling, mental health support, and recovery services designed to help individuals with opioid use disorder break the cycle of addiction.

"When the CORE program started, there was a lot of skepticism about the initiative," said EMS CORE Program Supervisor Joey Kerman. "Some said we would be lucky if we got 50 patients to recover from addiction." Kerman said the program has since exceeded multiple internal goals, reaching 100 patients, then 250, and now 850. "These 850 individuals have been able to reclaim their lives from the grips of addiction," he said.

The program relies on partnerships with Community Health Northwest Florida and Lakeview Center to deliver personalized, non-judgmental support at critical moments of intervention. Kerman emphasized that the county's approach focuses on reducing demand for drugs rather than arrest alone. "We knew Escambia County could not arrest its way out of our overdose problems," he said. "Our numbers prove that the CORE program and its local partners are helping people get off opioids."

For more information, residents can visit MyEscambia.com/CORE or contact CORE at 850-477-HELP or 850-377-4965.

item.title: Mayor Reeves: Family Sacrifices Central to Public Service
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Mayor DC Reeves emphasized Wednesday that his family plays an integral role in his ability to serve Pensacola, with loved ones directly participating in his official duties and sharing in the personal sacrifices required by the position. During an interview on the Pensacola Morning News, Reeves highlighted how his daughter Caroline participated in…
item.content:encoded:
Mayor DC Reeves emphasized Wednesday that his family plays an integral role in his ability to serve Pensacola, with loved ones directly participating in his official duties and sharing in the personal sacrifices required by the position.

During an interview on the Pensacola Morning News, Reeves highlighted how his daughter Caroline participated in the pledge of allegiance during official proceedings, while his brothers were involved in the swearing-in ceremony—underscoring the family-centered approach to his tenure.

"My family is integral to this role," Reeves said, noting that the constant demands of the mayoral office extend far beyond his own schedule and responsibilities.

The mayor acknowledged that public service at the municipal level requires significant personal commitments from entire households, not just the elected official. The job's unpredictable nature and ongoing community needs mean family members often adjust their own plans to accommodate the mayor's responsibilities.

Reeves' comments reflect a broader reality facing elected officials in Pensacola and across the nation: the blurred line between public duty and private life. His willingness to include family members in official moments serves as both a practical necessity and symbolic reminder of the interconnected nature of public service.

The mayor's remarks came during a wide-ranging discussion about city operations and community challenges. His emphasis on family involvement suggests a management philosophy that acknowledges the holistic demands placed on those in leadership positions.

As Reeves continues his tenure, the involvement of his family underscores a commitment to transparency about the true costs of public service in modern America.

item.title: Mayor Reeves Defends Debris Chipping Site Locations Amid Community Pushback
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Mayor D.C. Reeves addressed community criticism over debris chipping site locations during a Wednesday interview on the Pensacola Morning News, defending the city's decision to place facilities in locations that maximize efficiency while acknowledging resident concerns. One site location outside city limits near Barrancas drew particular scrutiny…
item.content:encoded:
Mayor D.C. Reeves addressed community criticism over debris chipping site locations during a Wednesday interview on the Pensacola Morning News, defending the city's decision to place facilities in locations that maximize efficiency while acknowledging resident concerns.

One site location outside city limits near Barrancas drew particular scrutiny from residents uncomfortable with its proximity to their neighborhoods. Reeves explained the city contracted experienced vendors to manage the debris removal process and faces new permitting requirements that complicate site selection.

"It's kind of nimbyism in a different way," Reeves said. "I want the savings, I want the cutback. I just didn't want that one, you know, but everybody's going to have that one that they're going to be upset about."

The mayor emphasized that the city must balance geographic efficiency with resident inconvenience when selecting cleanup locations. He noted that all debris chipping sites will close within weeks as debris piles have passed their peaks.

Reeves indicated the city plans to hold town halls to keep residents informed and hear their concerns and suggestions about the cleanup effort. The temporary nature of the sites underscores the city's commitment to removing storm debris while managing the operational challenges of coordinating multiple chipping facilities across the region.

The mayor's comments come as Pensacola continues recovery efforts following recent storm damage that generated significant debris requiring professional removal and processing.

item.title: Century Mayor, Council Member Meet with Youth Sports Leaders Over 'Pay To Play' Plan
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Century officials held a reassurance meeting Monday night with local youth sports leaders as backlash continues over a potential fee structure for town parks and facilities. According to NorthEscambia.com, Mayor Ben Boutwell and council member John Bass met with representatives from youth sports organizations after a November 17 report revealed…
item.content:encoded:
Century officials held a reassurance meeting Monday night with local youth sports leaders as backlash continues over a potential fee structure for town parks and facilities.

According to NorthEscambia.com, Mayor Ben Boutwell and council member John Bass met with representatives from youth sports organizations after a November 17 report revealed that town officials had been discussing charging leagues for utilities, field use, and park supplies—a move that sparked community concern.

Details on what reassurances were offered or whether the town plans to modify its approach were not immediately available. The meeting appears to have been an effort by town leadership to address concerns from youth sports organizers who rely on affordable access to municipal facilities.
